519.title: Depart from me (Luke 5:1–11)
519.hook: after the huge catch, Peter falls down: I'm a sinful man; Jesus says fear not
519.howItsDone: Christians read the great catch of fish as the call of the first disciples, and some churches use "launch out into the deep" to encourage people to begin something new in faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a doorway in Capernaum at sunset, and your line, every one of them.

Simon has been up all night with nothing to show for it: sore arms, cold hands, empty nets. He and his partners are on the shore, washing their nets, the last chore before sleep. A crowd is pressing in on a teacher by the water, so close he steps into Simon's boat and asks him to push off a little. Jesus sits and teaches from the boat. Then he turns to the tired fisherman and says something no fisherman wants to hear at the end of a bad night: let's go out again.
screen: `A NIGHT SHIFT WITH NOTHING TO SHOW.`

segments.voice: "Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught." Simon's answer, in the King James words, is tired and honest at once: "Master, we have toiled all the night, and have taken nothing: nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net." Nevertheless. That one word holds his exhaustion and his trust. The nets fill so full they start to tear. They wave to their partners in the other boat, and both boats fill until they begin to sink. You'd expect Simon to celebrate. Instead, "he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord." Go away from me. In Luke's telling, Simon looks at what just happened, then at himself, and wants distance. People still do something like it: when kindness comes unexpectedly, some of us deflect, or joke, or say you shouldn't have. Jesus doesn't argue about whether Simon is a sinner. He doesn't go away either. He says: "Fear not; from henceforth thou shalt catch men." Luke's Greek word for catch here is zogreo, which lexicons give as to take alive. Not fish for the market: catching to keep alive, the way you pull someone out of the water. And Luke ends: "they forsook all, and followed him." Two boats full of fish, left on the beach.
screen: `DEPART FROM ME; I AM A SINFUL MAN.`
then, large: `FEAR NOT; FROM HENCEFORTH THOU SHALT CATCH MEN.`

segments.voice: Think of a kindness you pushed away: a compliment you argued with, a gift you said was too much, help you refused because you didn't want to owe anyone. Notice the small voice that says depart from me, I don't deserve this, then picture that kindness coming again and let it land. If you pray, you can hear Jesus' answer to Simon as if it were spoken to you, fear not; if you don't, simply let the kindness stay.
Zogreo, Luke's Greek word for catching alive: Simon's cry after the great catch, overwhelmed by goodness, and the answer he gets instead, fear not.
Your line: fear not. Goodness doesn't have to be pushed away, even when it surprises you. See you tomorrow.

520.title: Take up your bed (Luke 5:12–26)
520.hook: a leper touched, and a man let through a roof by friends
520.carry: we have seen strange things today
520.howItsDone: Many Christians point to the friends on the roof when they pray for others or help someone who can't help themselves, sometimes called carrying someone in prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a tired fisherman, a tearing net, and your line, fear not.

Two people today can't get close to Jesus on their own. The first is a man "full of leprosy," as Luke puts it. In the Bible, leprosy covers a range of skin diseases, and it meant living apart, kept at a distance from family and worship. He falls on his face: "Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean." Not can you. If you want to. And Jesus "put forth his hand, and touched him." Before the healing, the touch, maybe the first the man had felt in years. The second person is lying on a mat in a house so crowded no one can get in the door.

Jesus is teaching inside, and the room is packed with teachers of the law from Galilee, Judea, even Jerusalem. Some men arrive carrying their paralyzed friend on a bed, and can't get through the crowd. So they climb onto the roof and, in the King James words, "let him down through the tiling with his couch into the midst before Jesus." Dust falling, tiles lifted, a mat swaying down on ropes into the middle of a lecture. Then: "And when he saw their faith, he said unto him, Man, thy sins are forgiven thee." Their faith. The friends'. The man on the mat may not have said a word. The teachers ask a serious question, and a fair one from their scriptures: "Who can forgive sins, but God alone?" Jesus answers by doing the visible thing so they'll believe the invisible one: "Arise, and take up thy couch, and go into thine house." The man stands, picks up the bed that carried him, and walks home praising God. And the whole room in one line: "We have seen strange things to day." The Greek is paradoxa, things contrary to what anyone expected, where English gets paradox. Christians see in this scene who Jesus is. Anyone can see in it what good friends are.
screen: then, large: `WE HAVE SEEN STRANGE THINGS TO DAY.`

segments.voice: Picture the friends on the roof, lifting tiles, lowering the ropes slowly, and let one person come to mind who can't get where they need to be on their own right now: a ride, a hand with a form, or just carrying for a while because they're too tired to walk. Ask whether there's a way around the crowd, a call or a door you could open. If you pray, you can carry that person to God in your mind; if you don't, simply carry them in your thoughts.
Paradoxa, Luke's Greek word for strange things, beyond all expecting: a paralyzed man's friends lower him through a roof, and he rises, takes up his own bed, and walks home.
Your line: we have seen strange things today. Sometimes the strange thing is a friend who won't give up. Day five hundred twenty, done.

521.title: The new wine (Luke 5:27–39)
521.hook: Levi's big feast, and no one after drinking old wine wants new
521.howItsDone: Christians remember Levi as Matthew, the tax collector who became an apostle, and many churches read the call of Levi as a picture of welcome at the table.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a hole in a roof, a man carrying his own bed, and your line, we have seen strange things today.

A tax booth on a road near the lake. Levi sits behind it, collecting customs on goods passing through. Steady money, and it does not make him popular. Earlier in Luke, John the Baptist tells tax collectors to collect no more than they're owed, which says something about their reputation. Jesus walks up and says two words: "Follow me." And Luke says, "he left all, rose up, and followed him." No negotiation. Then Levi does what people do when their life changes overnight: he throws a big party in his own house and invites everyone he knows. For a tax collector, that means a lot of other tax collectors.

Some Pharisees and their scribes ask the disciples: "Why do ye eat and drink with publicans and sinners?" For them, a shared table was a sign of belonging, and they took holiness seriously. Jesus answers: "They that are whole need not a physician; but they that are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." Then they ask about fasting: John's disciples fast, yours eat and drink. Jesus answers with pictures from the kitchen. Nobody tears a patch from a new coat to fix an old one. Nobody pours new wine into old wineskins: "else the new wine will burst the bottles, and be spilled." Bottles here are wineskins, leather bags. New wine is still fermenting, still stretching; an old skin, already stiff, can't give, and it splits. "But new wine must be put into new bottles; and both are preserved." Something new needs room to grow. Then a last line, almost a joke: "No man also having drunk old wine straightway desireth new: for he saith, The old is better." We like what we know. Readers have heard this many ways: some as gentle patience with people slow to change, others as a wry smile at how hard change is. Levi changed overnight. Others take longer. The text seems to make room for both.
screen: then, large: `NEW WINE MUST BE PUT INTO NEW BOTTLES.`

segments.voice: Think of something new you've wanted to start, a few minutes of quiet in the morning, a walk, an earlier bedtime, and notice the part of you that says the old way is fine; that's not a villain, just old wine talking. Picture the smallest new skin you could make room for, one minute instead of thirty, something that can stretch as it grows. If you pray, you can ask for patience with your own pace; if you don't, simply let the small new thing feel welcome.
Wineskins. The leather bags Jesus says new wine needs: old ones, already stretched stiff, split; new ones give the wine room to grow.
Your line: new wine takes time. Slow change still counts as change. That's day five hundred twenty-one.

522.title: All night on the mountain (Luke 6:1–16)
522.hook: before choosing the twelve, he prays all night
522.howItsDone: Christians often pray before major decisions, and some keep a night or a day of prayer before an important choice, remembering Jesus' night on the mountain.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Levi's feast, new wine, and your line, new wine takes time.

How do you make a choice that will shape everything after it? A job, a move, who to trust. Some people make lists, some ask friends, some lie awake at three in the morning, scrolling. Luke shows Jesus making one: picking the small group who would carry his work after him. The chapter starts with arguments: disciples picking grain on the sabbath, a man with a withered hand healed in a synagogue, tempers rising over what the sabbath is for. Jesus asks: is it lawful on the sabbath to do good, or to do evil? Then, before the choice, he leaves the noise behind and climbs.
screen: `HOW DO YOU MAKE A BIG CHOICE?`

segments.voice: In the King James words: "And it came to pass in those days, that he went out into a mountain to pray, and continued all night in prayer to God." All night. Hours in the dark, on a hillside, alone. Luke keeps showing Jesus at prayer: at his baptism, in lonely places, before Peter names him the Christ, on another mountain before his face changes. In Luke, prayer turns up at the turning points. Then: "And when it was day, he called unto him his disciples: and of them he chose twelve, whom also he named apostles." The Greek is apostolos, someone sent out, an envoy. Twelve, and many readers hear an echo of the twelve tribes of Israel. Luke gives the names: Simon, whom he named Peter, and Andrew his brother; James and John; Philip and Bartholomew; Matthew and Thomas; James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon called the Zealot; Judas the brother of James, and Judas Iscariot, "which also was the traitor." A whole night of prayer, and the list still includes the man who will betray him. Luke doesn't explain that, and doesn't try. What the text does show: praying first didn't guarantee an easy outcome. In Luke's telling, the choice was made in prayer, eyes open, at dawn.
screen: `JUDAS TOO, AFTER A NIGHT OF PRAYER.`
then, large: `HE CONTINUED ALL NIGHT IN PRAYER TO GOD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a decision in front of you, and don't solve it or run the pros and cons again; just hold it, the way you'd hold a stone in your hand, feeling its weight, what you fear and what you hope. Let the quiet do some of the work the lists can't. If you pray, you can bring the choice to God without asking for an answer yet; if you don't, simply hold it in silence and see what rises.
Apostolos, Greek for one who is sent out, an envoy: the name Jesus gives the twelve, chosen at dawn after he prayed through the night alone on a hillside.
Your line: pray first. Even a whole night of prayer didn't make the road easy. Rest well, and see you tomorrow.

523.title: The plain (Luke 6:17–26)
523.hook: Luke's beatitudes: blessed are you poor, and woe to you who are rich
523.tomorrow: give, and it will be given
523.howItsDone: Christians often read Luke's Sermon on the Plain alongside Matthew's Sermon on the Mount, and some churches and charities draw on Luke 6:20–21 in their work with the poor and hungry.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a night of prayer on the mountain, twelve chosen at dawn, and your line, pray first.

In Matthew, the Beatitudes come from a mountain: Jesus goes up, sits down, and teaches. Luke tells it differently, starting with the ground. After the night of prayer, Jesus comes down with the twelve and "stood in the plain." The Greek means a level place. Not above the crowd; on the same ground as everyone. And the crowd is huge and mixed, from Judea and Jerusalem, and from the coast of Tyre and Sidon, outside Israel, pushing forward to touch him, because, Luke says, power was coming out of him and healing them all. Then he looks at his disciples, and starts to speak.

In the King James words: "Blessed be ye poor: for yours is the kingdom of God. Blessed are ye that hunger now: for ye shall be filled. Blessed are ye that weep now: for ye shall laugh." Three things. First, Luke says you: blessed are you poor, spoken to the hungry and crying people in front of him. Second, the word now. Hungry now, weeping now; this isn't the final word on their lives. Third, Matthew has poor in spirit, and Luke simply ye poor. Christians read the two side by side. Some stress actual poverty, as in the Catholic teaching sometimes called the preferential option for the poor; others stress the humble heart that knows it needs God. Then Luke does something Matthew doesn't: he turns the blessings over, and on the other side are woes. "But woe unto you that are rich! for ye have received your consolation. Woe unto you that are full! for ye shall hunger. Woe unto you that laugh now! for ye shall mourn and weep." Four blessings, four woes, like a coin with two faces. Woe in Greek is ouai, a cry rather than a curse; some readers hear it as alas, a warning said with sorrow. The blessed in Luke are the hungry and the grieving, the ones on level ground. And the comfortable are warned, sadly, that comfort can become all the reward there is.
screen: then, large: `BLESSED BE YE POOR: FOR YOURS IS THE KINGDOM OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Picture your own neighborhood or commute, and ask who is hungry now, who is weeping now, who people step around: the man outside the grocery store, the coworker who's been quiet since the funeral. Hold each face for a breath, and ask gently what it would mean to stand on level ground with them. If you pray, you can hold them before God; if you don't, simply see them.
The plain. In Luke, Jesus teaches the Beatitudes on a level place, speaking to the poor, the hungry and the weeping as you, and adding four woes.
Your line: blessed are you poor. In Luke, the blessing is spoken on level ground. Day five hundred twenty-three.

524.title: Give, and it will be given (Luke 6:27–38)
524.hook: good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over
524.howItsDone: Christians often read Luke 6:38 as a call to generous giving, alongside the Golden Rule in Luke 6:31.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the level place, four blessings and four woes, and your line, blessed are you poor.

At a grain market, you hold out your measure, a basket or a jar. A stingy seller fills it loosely, full of air pockets, and levels it off flat. A generous one pours the grain in, presses it down with his hand, shakes the container so it settles, pours in more, and keeps going until it's heaped and spilling over the sides, and you hold out the fold of your robe to catch the rest. That's the picture Jesus ends this teaching with. But first, he says some very hard things.

Still on the level place, in the King James words: "Love your enemies, do good to them which hate you, Bless them that curse you, and pray for them which despitefully use you." Turn the other cheek. Give to everyone who asks. Lend, hoping for nothing back. And the line now called the Golden Rule: "as ye would that men should do to you, do ye also to them likewise." Then the center of it all: "Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful." Mercy is the measure. And the picture from the market: "Give, and it shall be given unto you; good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over, shall men give into your bosom." Bosom here isn't your chest. The Greek word, kolpos, can mean the lap or the fold of a robe, which could hold grain like a pouch. A lap overflowing. Then the hinge: "For with the same measure that ye mete withal it shall be measured to you again." Mete means to measure out. This isn't a get-rich promise; a few lines earlier, Jesus told people to lend, hoping for nothing again. The measure is about mercy: judge not, condemn not, forgive, give, and the same measure comes back. The basket you hold out to others is the basket you're handed. Running over.
screen: then, large: `GIVE, AND IT SHALL BE GIVEN UNTO YOU.`

segments.voice: Picture your hands as the seller's hands, holding a basket, and think of someone you could give to: money, maybe, or time, praise, patience, a long phone call. Notice the first instinct to level it off, then picture pressing it down, shaking it together, adding a bit more: a longer visit, a real compliment instead of a quick one. If you pray, you can ask for open hands; if you don't, simply picture the basket overflowing.
Give. Jesus' teaching on the plain: be merciful, give without counting, and what you give comes back pressed down, shaken together and running over.
Your line: running over. Pressed down, shaken together, spilling into your lap. Day five hundred twenty-four, and counting.

525.title: Blind guides (Luke 6:39–49)
525.hook: a good person out of the good treasure of the heart brings good
525.carry: out of the heart the mouth speaks
525.howItsDone: Christians often quote the mote and the beam as a check before judging others, and the house built on the rock is a familiar Sunday school song and sermon picture.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a grain market, a heaped measure, and your line, running over.

"Can the blind lead the blind? shall they not both fall into the ditch?" Jesus says it almost like a riddle, the kind of saying you'd hear at a village well. It's the last stretch of the sermon on the plain, and the tone changes. After love your enemies and the heaped measure, he turns to the people who guide others: parents, teachers, bosses, friends who give advice. Which is everyone. And he offers quick pictures, one after another: a ditch, a speck of dust, a fig tree, a storehouse, a house in a flood.
screen: `A DITCH, A SPECK, A TREE, A HOUSE.`

segments.voice: First, the speck: "And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but perceivest not the beam that is in thine own eye?" A mote is a speck of dust. A beam is a wooden roof beam. The picture is meant to be funny: a man with a plank sticking out of his face, squinting at his friend's eyelash. Fix your own sight first. Second, the tree: "For of thorns men do not gather figs, nor of a bramble bush gather they grapes." You judge a tree by what grows on it. Third, the heart: "A good man out of the good treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is good; and an evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is evil: for of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaketh." Treasure here is thesauros, a storehouse. Whatever you've been storing comes out when you open your mouth. Words are the fruit; the heart is the tree. Last, the house. Someone who hears and does is like a man who "digged deep, and laid the foundation on a rock." The flood comes, and the house stands. Someone who hears and doesn't do built on bare earth, and the flood takes it. So the blind guide isn't someone without sight. It's someone who hasn't looked inward, who talks without doing.
screen: `A TREE IS KNOWN BY ITS FRUIT.`
then, large: `OF THE ABUNDANCE OF THE HEART HIS MOUTH SPEAKETH.`

segments.voice: Picture your heart as a storehouse, shelves and barrels, and look honestly at what's been stored this week: worry, gratitude, a grudge, a kind thing someone said. Then find something good on those shelves, a memory of kindness or something that made you laugh, and hold it for a few breaths. If you pray, you can ask for a good storehouse; if you don't, simply rest with the good thing you found.
Blind guides. Jesus' warning about guiding others without looking inward first, and his picture of words coming out of the storehouse of the heart.

Your line: out of the heart the mouth speaks. A week of a tearing net, a hole in a roof, new wine, a night of prayer, the plain, a heaped measure and a storehouse. Day five hundred twenty-five, and another week on the path.
